Vitamin E deficiency neuropathy

[THOUGHT] The proposed diagnosis is vitamin E deficiency neuropathy (more accurately, vitamin E deficiency–associated spinocerebellar ataxia). While this is a highly plausible and clinically appropriate consideration—given the patient’s Crohn disease (a known cause of fat malabsorption), gait ataxia, and absence of red-flag neurological symptoms or alternative micronutrient deficiencies (B12, copper)—**vitamin E level has not yet been measured**. Since vitamin E deficiency is biochemical (not clinical) by definition—and neurologic manifestations can overlap with other causes (e.g., idiopathic cerebellar ataxia, MS, paraneoplastic syndromes, or even silent structural lesions)—diagnostic confirmation requires objective evidence of low serum α-tocopherol. With turns exhausted (6/6), no further data acquisition is possible. [DECISION] INCOMPLETE

[FEEDBACK] Serum α-tocopherol (vitamin E) level is mandatory to confirm vitamin E deficiency; this test has not yet been reported or performed. Without this result, the diagnosis cannot be definitively established.

ANALYSIS: Progressive multifocal encephalopathy (PML) is a rare, demyelinating CNS infection caused by reactivation of the JC virus, typically in immunocompromised individuals. It presents with progressive neurological deficits and characteristic MRI findings (non-enhancing, asymmetric white matter lesions). Vitamin E deficiency neuropathy, in contrast, is a peripheral neuropathy caused by chronic vitamin E deficiency (e.g., due to malabsorption), manifesting with sensory ataxia, areflexia, and proprioceptive loss — not encephalopathy or white matter demyelination. The two conditions differ fundamentally in etiology, pathology, anatomical involvement (CNS vs. PNS), clinical presentation, and diagnostic workup. The predicted diagnosis is entirely unrelated and inconsistent with the reference diagnosis.
